pedagogy.summary: At age 12-14 pupils learn the classical ruler-and-compass constructions — perpendicular bisector of a segment, perpendicular to a line from/at a point, and angle bisector — using ONLY compasses and a straight edge, with no measuring of lengths or angles. The essential shift is from DRAWING (find a midpoint with a ruler, judge a right angle by eye or protractor) to CONSTRUCTING (produce the result from geometric properties). The unifying property is the rhombus: equal-radius arcs from two points create four equal lengths, so the figure is a rhombus, whose diagonals perpendicularly bisect each other and bisect their angles. Taught this way, every construction is a deduction, and the commonest error — changing the compass radius between the two endpoints — is instantly diagnosable: unequal radii give a KITE (diagonals perpendicular but NOT bisecting), so the line is perpendicular but misses the midpoint. Because compasses are usually new at KS3, motor coordination is a real, separable hurdle; developing the concept first with dynamic geometry lets pupils reason about 'perfect' circles before wrestling the physical tool.
bestPractices: Teach the draw-vs-construct distinction explicitly: a construction uses geometric properties (equidistance), not measurement; require pupils to leave their construction arcs as evidence of method
Anchor every construction in the rhombus/isosceles-triangle property (equal radii → rhombus → diagonals perpendicularly bisect and bisect the angle), so steps are deductions, not a memorised routine
Make the equal-radius rule meaningful via the kite counter-case: unequal arcs build a kite whose diagonals are perpendicular but do not bisect, so the midpoint is missed
Ensure the compass opening exceeds half the segment so the arcs intersect above and below; discuss why a smaller radius fails and a huge one is just wasteful

Present non-standard (diagonal, rotated) segments and angles, not only horizontal/vertical prototypes, and give time to build compass dexterity — ideally after establishing the idea with dynamic geometry
keyRepresentations: Two equal-radius circles/arcs from the segment ends and the rhombus they define
The rhombus-around-a-diagonal image (segment as one diagonal; the construction produces the other)
Kite counter-example (unequal radii) showing perpendicular-but-not-bisecting diagonals
Isosceles triangle whose altitude bisects the base at right angles and bisects the apex angle
commonMisconceptions: Changing the compass radius between the two endpoints, constructing a kite instead of a rhombus, so the line is perpendicular but does not pass through the midpoint
Drawing rather than constructing — using a ruler to find the midpoint and a protractor/eye for the right angle — and leaving no construction marks
Opening the compasses to less than half the segment, so the arcs never intersect
Memorising the steps as an isolated routine with no link to the properties of circles and rhombuses
Treating the construction as valid only for horizontal/vertical segments (prototype-orientation bias)

learn.summary: Pupils aged 12–14 construct a perpendicular bisector, a perpendicular to a line from a point off it or at a point on it, and an angle bisector using compasses and an unmarked straight edge. Explain the equal-distance and congruent-triangle properties, leaving arcs visible rather than finding positions by measurement. Equal-radius circles centred at segment endpoints yield a perpendicular bisector; unequal radii can still give a perpendicular common chord, but it misses the segment midpoint. Optional dynamic geometry can separate reasoning from tool dexterity; physical compass practice remains part of the proposed tasks. Verification by measurement may check accuracy afterwards, but it does not justify the construction.

activities.title: Construct the perpendicular bisector with compasses and straight edge
feedback: If the line does not cross PQ at its midpoint, check whether the two sets of arcs have equal radii: unequal radii make a KITE (the line is perpendicular to PQ but does not bisect it), equal radii make a rhombus (the line is perpendicular to PQ AND bisects it).

If equal-radius arcs do not cross at two points, check the opening: below half PQ they do not meet; at exactly half they touch only at the midpoint. Use an opening greater than half PQ and allow enough space on the page.

If there are no arcs on the page and the midpoint was found with a ruler or the angle judged by eye, that is drawing, not constructing: redo it so every point of the line is equidistant from P and Q, shown by equal arcs.
Keeping the compass width unchanged between P and Q is the whole point — it is what forces the rhombus.
activities.rationale: Constructing is a doing-and-reasoning skill: pupils must physically execute equal-radius arcs and justify them from the rhombus/equidistance property. A finished static picture cannot be manipulated and does not require the pupil to perform the arcs or articulate the reasoning, so it serves at most as a labelled reference for the rhombus property. Leaving arcs visible makes the method inspectable and distinguishes construction from measurement.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'use the standard ruler and compass constructions (perpendicular bisector of a line segment, constructing a perpendicular to a given line from/at a given point, bisecting a given angle); recognise and use the perpendicular distance from a point to a line as the shortest distance to the line'.

A construction uses geometric properties, not measurement; changing the compass radius between endpoints builds a KITE not a rhombus, and a kite's diagonals are perpendicular but do not bisect, so no perpendicular bisector results (the 'Tinashe' example); the radius must exceed half the segment for the arcs to intersect; constructions should be linked to circle/rhombus properties rather than memorised, presented in non-standard orientations, and compass dexterity is a new KS3 hurdle (aim within ±2 mm/±2°).
learnerActions: Take a line segment PQ drawn diagonally (not horizontal or vertical), a pair of compasses and a straight edge — no ruler measuring and no protractor.
Open the compasses to MORE than half of PQ; discuss why an opening of half or less means the arcs only touch or never meet, and why an enormous opening just wastes space.
Place the compass point on P and sweep an arc above and below the segment; WITHOUT changing the radius, place the point on Q and sweep again so the arcs cross at two points.
Rule the straight line through the two crossing points, leaving all construction arcs visible as evidence of method.
Explain why the line passes through the midpoint at 90°: the four equal radii form a rhombus, whose diagonals perpendicularly bisect each other.
Repeat on segments at several different orientations, not only horizontal/vertical ones.
activities.intendedInsight: Every point on the perpendicular bisector is equidistant from P and Q. Equal-radius arcs locate two such points, and the straight line through them is the perpendicular bisector; visible arcs make the method inspectable, though arcs alone do not prove they were placed correctly.

activities.title: Bisect an angle using the same equal-arc idea
feedback: If the line does not appear to split the angle equally, check that the two inner arcs were drawn with the same radius from each arm-crossing point.

Leave your arcs visible — they show you constructed the bisector from equal lengths rather than measuring halves with a protractor. (The congruent halves follow from the equal arcs, so no measuring is needed to justify it.)
activities.rationale: Equal lengths and congruent triangles provide the justification for the angle bisector. After constructing, measuring both angles can be an optional check of drawing accuracy; it is not the construction method or a proof. This is a proposed property-based activity, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'use the standard ruler and compass constructions (perpendicular bisector of a line segment, constructing a perpendicular to a given line from/at a given point, bisecting a given angle); recognise and use the perpendicular distance from a point to a line as the shortest distance to the line'.

A construction uses geometric properties, not measurement; changing the compass radius between endpoints builds a KITE not a rhombus, and a kite's diagonals are perpendicular but do not bisect, so no perpendicular bisector results (the 'Tinashe' example); the radius must exceed half the segment for the arcs to intersect; constructions should be linked to circle/rhombus properties rather than memorised, presented in non-standard orientations, and compass dexterity is a new KS3 hurdle (aim within ±2 mm/±2°).
learnerActions: Take a marked angle (try one at a non-standard orientation), compasses and a straight edge.
Place the compass point at the vertex and sweep an arc that crosses both arms of the angle at two points.
WITHOUT changing the radius, place the point on each of those two crossing points in turn and sweep equal arcs that meet inside the angle.
Rule the line from the vertex through that meeting point, leaving the arcs visible.
Explain how this reuses the equal-radius property: equal lengths from the vertex and equal arcs from the arm-crossings force the two halves to be congruent, so the line bisects the angle.
activities.intendedInsight: The same equidistance principle that bisects a segment also bisects an angle — one property, reused, rather than a second memorised routine.

activities.title: See the rhombus break into a kite with a dynamic compass (concept-before-dexterity scaffold)
feedback: When the figure flips to KITE, note exactly where the line crosses PQ relative to the midpoint — that gap is why unequal radii fail.
If you can state why the rhombus's crossing line bisects PQ but the kite's does not, you are reasoning from the property; move on to building the same construction by hand.
activities.rationale: A dynamic-geometry tool can separate the concept (equidistance locus, rhombus-vs-kite) from manual dexterity, and may let pupils reason about ideal 'perfect' circles before coping with the practical difficulties of real compasses, which some pupils may still find hard to control. The live slider and label flip are intended to make the failure mode concrete. This is a proposed scaffold: it does not develop the manual construction skill, which must be practised separately on paper, and its effectiveness over other media is untested.
sourceClaims: A construction uses geometric properties, not measurement; changing the compass radius between endpoints builds a KITE not a rhombus, and a kite's diagonals are perpendicular but do not bisect, so no perpendicular bisector results (the 'Tinashe' example); the radius must exceed half the segment for the arcs to intersect; constructions should be linked to circle/rhombus properties rather than memorised, presented in non-standard orientations, and compass dexterity is a new KS3 hurdle (aim within ±2 mm/±2°).
learnerActions: Use an on-screen compass whose radius locks once set: plant it on P and sweep an arc, then on Q and sweep an equal arc so the two equal circles cross at two points.
Rule the line through the crossings and observe the highlighted locus showing every point on it is equidistant from P and Q.

Now drag a slider that shrinks the second circle's radius (keeping it large enough that the two circles still cross); watch the crossing points drift, the line slide sideways while staying perpendicular to PQ, and the label flip from RHOMBUS to KITE — the line visibly misses the midpoint.
Articulate in your own words why 'keep the compass fixed' is a consequence of the rhombus property, not an arbitrary rule.
Transfer to real compasses and paper once the concept is secure.
activities.intendedInsight: When two circles cross, their common chord is perpendicular to the line through their centres. With equal radii, that chord also bisects PQ; with unequal radii it does not. Keep both circles crossing during the comparison, and explain the equal-radius rule rather than memorising it.

activities.title: Diagnose: construction or drawing? Which radius? Which shape failed?
feedback: For the 8 cm segment, any opening at or below 4 cm leaves arcs that cannot cross on both sides (at exactly 4 cm they only touch at the midpoint); the opening must exceed half the length.
The diagram with no arcs cannot be shown to be a construction — without equal arcs there is no evidence the equidistance property was used.
Unequal arcs give a kite: perpendicular, yes, but the line through the crossings does not bisect PQ (only PQ bisects it), so the line misses the midpoint.
activities.rationale: Questions of this kind assess the reasoning behind the construction and surface the specific misconceptions (radius too small, kite error, drawing vs constructing). They complement but cannot replace the performance task, since recognising a correct diagram is not the same as producing one.
sourceClaims: A construction uses geometric properties, not measurement; changing the compass radius between endpoints builds a KITE not a rhombus, and a kite's diagonals are perpendicular but do not bisect, so no perpendicular bisector results (the 'Tinashe' example); the radius must exceed half the segment for the arcs to intersect; constructions should be linked to circle/rhombus properties rather than memorised, presented in non-standard orientations, and compass dexterity is a new KS3 hurdle (aim within ±2 mm/±2°).
learnerActions: For an 8 cm segment, choose which compass opening will work for the perpendicular bisector (more than 4 cm) and say why openings of 4 cm or less fail.

Compare a diagram with visible equal-radius construction arcs with a bare line. Explain which supplies evidence of the method and which does not; a bare line alone does not reveal whether someone constructed it and erased the arcs or drew it by measurement.

Given a diagram where the line is perpendicular to PQ but misses the midpoint, name the shape that was built (a kite) and explain why the line through the arc crossings does not bisect PQ, even though PQ bisects that line.

Answer: Why must the compass stay the same width from both P and Q, and what shape are you really making? How does the same equal-arc idea bisect an angle? Why would a ruler-and-protractor method not count as a construction?
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to diagnose the radius condition, the kite failure, and construction-vs-drawing demonstrates understanding of the underlying properties — though recognising a correct diagram does not substitute for executing the construction by hand.

activities.title: Construct a perpendicular from a point off a line
feedback: If the circle centred at A only touches l or misses it, increase the radius until it meets l twice. A single touch does not provide distinct B and C for this construction.
If an arc crossing coincides with A, use the other crossing, or adjust the common radius so D is distinct from A; two distinct points are needed to draw AD.
If the perpendicular does not pass through A, return to the given point and the equidistance argument. A perpendicular somewhere else on the line does not meet this task.
activities.rationale: This editorially added construction covers the explicit curriculum objective missing from the saved activities. It reuses the perpendicular-bisector equidistance reasoning; the specific procedure is a proposed task rather than an empirically tested design.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'use the standard ruler and compass constructions (perpendicular bisector of a line segment, constructing a perpendicular to a given line from/at a given point, bisecting a given angle); recognise and use the perpendicular distance from a point to a line as the shortest distance to the line'.
learnerActions: Draw a line l and a point A not on it. With centre A, choose a compass radius large enough for a circle to cross l at two distinct points B and C; extend l with the straight edge if needed.
Using equal radii from B and C, each greater than half BC, draw crossing arcs to locate a point D off l and distinct from A. Draw the straight line through A and D, keeping the arcs visible.
Explain why AB = AC and DB = DC place both A and D on the perpendicular bisector of BC. Since B and C lie on l, AD is perpendicular to l. Mark the foot H where AD meets l.
Explain that AH is the shortest distance from A to l. Repeat with a rotated line and A on the other side.
activities.intendedInsight: A point equidistant from B and C lies on their perpendicular bisector. Finding a second distinct equidistant point locates a perpendicular through the given off-line point without measuring a right angle.

activities.title: Construct a perpendicular at a point on a line
feedback: If B and C are not equally far from A, redraw them using the same circle centred at A; estimating their positions by eye does not establish that A is the midpoint.
If the arcs from B and C fail to cross away from l, increase their common radius beyond half BC.
A measured 90° angle can be an accuracy check, but explain the equal distances to justify why the construction works.
activities.rationale: This editorial addition covers the at-a-point case of the named objective and connects it to the already taught perpendicular bisector. It does not claim measured educational effectiveness.
sourceClaims: KS3 statutory: pupils 'use the standard ruler and compass constructions (perpendicular bisector of a line segment, constructing a perpendicular to a given line from/at a given point, bisecting a given angle); recognise and use the perpendicular distance from a point to a line as the shortest distance to the line'.
learnerActions: Draw a line l with a given point A on it. Draw a circle centred at A to mark B and C on l, on opposite sides of A, so AB = AC.
Without changing the compass opening between B and C, draw equal-radius arcs from them, using a radius greater than half BC, to meet at D off l.
Rule AD and leave the arcs visible. Explain that A is the midpoint of BC and both A and D are equidistant from B and C, so AD is the perpendicular bisector of BC and is perpendicular to l at A.

Try a sloping line and then explain how this task differs from constructing a perpendicular through a point off the line. After the construction, a protractor can check practical accuracy without replacing the property-based justification.
activities.intendedInsight: The given point on the line can be made the midpoint of a constructed segment BC, so its perpendicular bisector passes through that point.

constraints: Use compasses and an unmarked straight edge to locate the required points and lines from geometric properties, rather than by measuring. A ruler or protractor may check practical accuracy afterwards; such checks do not prove or replace the construction.
Require pupils to leave their construction arcs visible as evidence that the equidistance/rhombus property, not measurement, produced the result.
Keep the compass width unchanged between the two endpoints, and open it to more than half the segment so the arcs intersect above and below.
Present segments and angles at non-standard (diagonal, rotated) orientations, not only horizontal/vertical prototypes.

A dynamic-geometry compass is a concept-building scaffold: it may help pupils reason about equidistance and the rhombus-vs-kite distinction but does not develop the manual dexterity, which must be practised with real compasses afterwards.
Recognition/multiple-choice items assess the reasoning only; they do not evidence the pupil actually executing the construction, which is the performance target.

Treat tolerances such as ±2 mm / ±2° as accuracy targets for the manual skill, distinguishing a dexterity lapse (correct method, slipped arcs) from a conceptual error (unequal radii, measuring instead of constructing).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated a static picture and 3D as 'poor' and asserted '3D adds nothing' and that a static picture 'cannot build' the reasoning. These universal comparative claims are replaced here with narrow affordances (a fixed image cannot be manipulated and does not elicit the pupil executing arcs; recognition items do not elicit independent construction). These constructions are planar, so a 3D medium is simply not needed for the 2D locus reasoning; a labelled reference image can still support recall of the rhombus property.

Geometry self-audit: the rhombus/kite reasoning is internally consistent — equal radii from both endpoints give four equal sides (a rhombus) whose diagonals perpendicularly bisect; unequal radii give a kite (axis of symmetry PQ) with perpendicular diagonals, where PQ bisects the constructed line but the constructed line does NOT bisect PQ, so it misses the segment's midpoint. No arithmetic or force/motion content to correct. The 8 cm example (opening must exceed 4 cm, and exactly 4 cm only touches at the midpoint) is correct.

Paper diagrams are flat representations of ideal plane constructions; no solid-shape idealisation issue arises here, but treat drawn arcs as physical approximations of ideal circles when discussing tolerance.

The saved activities omitted perpendiculars from or at a given point even though the objective names them. Two conservative editorial activities now cover these cases using the perpendicular-bisector equidistance property. Original pedagogy and assessment remain unchanged.

The original evidence suggests measuring the two angle halves. This is compatible with a post-construction accuracy check; the construction itself and its justification use equal lengths and congruent triangles, not measurement.

Useful factual-audit repairs retain the common-chord perpendicular direction, correct the kite diagonal scope, and keep circles intersecting in the slider activity. Source claims remain verbatim even where their compressed kite wording needs the qualification given in the activities. No fresh source verification was performed.

probeDeeper: Why must the compass stay open to the same width from both P and Q — what shape are you really making?
If someone changed the compass width and got a line perpendicular to PQ that isn't the bisector, what shape did they make, and why doesn't it bisect?
Could you do this with a ruler and protractor instead? Why would that not count as a construction?
How does the same equal-arc idea let you bisect an ANGLE?
assess.correctAnswer: Opens the compasses to more than half PQ and, WITHOUT changing the radius, draws equal arcs from P and from Q that intersect above and below, then rules the line through the two intersections — leaving the arcs visible; the line passes through the midpoint at 90° (within about ±2 mm / ±2°). For the angle, draws an arc from the vertex crossing both arms, then equal arcs from those two points, and rules the vertex-to-intersection line. Relies on the equal-radius (rhombus) property, not measurement.

errorPatterns.pattern: Changes the compass radius between the two endpoints, constructing a kite instead of a rhombus — so the line is perpendicular to PQ but does not pass through the midpoint (does not bisect)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reground on the rhombus property — four equal radii make a rhombus whose diagonals bisect; a kite's diagonals are perpendicular but do not bisect — and insist the compass width is unchanged between endpoints
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The arcs from P and from Q have visibly different radii, and the resulting line does not cross PQ at its midpoint

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws rather than constructs — uses a ruler to find the midpoint and a protractor or eye for the right angle — and leaves no construction arcs
errorPatterns.nextMove: Teach the draw-vs-construct distinction: a construction produces the result from geometric properties (equidistance), not measurement; require visible construction marks
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Measures PQ to mark its midpoint, judges 90° by eye/protractor, and the page shows a bare line with no arcs

errorPatterns.pattern: Opens the compasses to less than half the segment, so the arcs from P and Q never intersect
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish that the radius must exceed half the segment for the arcs to intersect on both sides; connect to the equidistant-locus reason
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The arcs fail to meet above and/or below the segment, leaving no crossing points to rule through

errorPatterns.pattern: Compass dexterity lapse — the method is right but the arcs slip or are placed imprecisely, so the construction falls outside tolerance
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: give practice time with the equipment (this is usually new at KS3) and consider establishing the concept first with dynamic geometry
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Equal radii and visible arcs, but the point/needle slipped and the result is off by more than ±2 mm / ±2°

responseLevels.gap: Cannot produce the construction from properties — measures the midpoint, judges the angle by eye, or changes the radius so it fails — with no sense of why it should work.
responseLevels.full: Constructs the perpendicular bisector and angle bisector from the equidistance/rhombus property — radius equal and more than half, arcs left visible, at any orientation — and explains why equal radii force a rhombus whose diagonals perpendicularly bisect.
responseLevels.partial: Executes the memorised steps and often gets a correct-looking bisector, but cannot explain why the equal radii are needed or link it to the rhombus/equidistance property — slips to a kite or to measuring when the orientation is unfamiliar.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a pair of compasses, a straight edge, and a line segment PQ drawn diagonally (not horizontal), plus a marked angle. Say: 'Construct the perpendicular bisector of PQ using only the compasses and straight edge — no ruler measuring and no protractor. Then construct the bisector of this angle.' Watch whether they keep the compass radius equal from both endpoints, open it to more than half PQ, leave their construction arcs, and work from properties rather than measuring.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The finished construction is the evidence: equal-radius arcs and a line through the midpoint show the child used the rhombus/equidistance property; unequal arcs (a kite whose line misses the midpoint), or a ruler-found midpoint with an eyeballed right angle and no arcs, show drawing rather than constructing. A correct property-based construction cannot be produced by measuring.
